title: Too Old to Benefit From FinTech ? An Exploratory Study on Older Adults' Access to and Adoption of Robo‐Advice
abstract: ABSTRACT Robo‐advice has the potential to provide affordable financial advice to assist older adults with building and managing retirement income. Yet robo‐advice uptake among those aged 60 to 80 years is low, and little is known about how they engage with robo‐advice. Our study examines the drivers and barriers to robo‐advice access and adoption among older adults, and provides practical recommendations for industry and policymakers. Drawing on qualitative surveys and interviews with academic and industry experts familiar with the Australian financial advice landscape. We identify six core themes and their possible interrelationships, which likely affect older adults' access and adoption: robo‐advice design, digital and financial capabilities, trust, psychological comfort, regulatory deficiencies, and social influence. In integrating our findings with the technology acceptance and financial planning literature, we construct a conceptual framework that responds to calls for more comprehensive explanations of consumer behavior toward robo‐advice.

title: Strengthening or Straining Resilience? Climate Risk Disclosure and Technology Adoption in Banks
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines bank digital transformation and climate risk disclosure as two concurrent strategic investments and tests their joint effect on market‐implied default risk, a question central to financial‐system resilience under SDG 13. Using a global sample of 543 listed banks from 2000 to 2023, we examine how technology‐firm acquisitions and climate risk disclosure relate to market‐implied default probability. title: How NBU’s Communications Have Changed During Full-Scale War: An AI Perspective
abstract: This study examines how the National Bank of Ukraine’s (NBU) communications have changed during the full-scale war. Using a large language model (LLM, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite), we classify each sentence of 43 Inflation Reports published in 2015–2026 as policy or nonpolicy communications. We then split policy communications into main objectives (price stability, financial stability, and economic activity), additional tasks (such as anchoring expectations or exchange rate considerations), and the rationales for policy decisions. abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the factors influencing financial technology (FinTech) adoption among Indian farmers by extending the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), with behavioral intention as a mediating mechanism. title: RehearsalBench: Can AI Predict What Happens When You Change a Company?
abstract: Organizations increasingly ask AI systems what will happen if they change how they operate: which work to automate, which team to resize, what a voice agent will do to waiting times. We introduce RehearsalBench, a benchmark that measures whether AI models can diagnose an operation, choose an intervention, and forecast its consequences. Each model is placed in a simulated bank contact center fitted to real call-level records, sees only what a manager would see, and submits a plan and forecasts that are then played out across 200 seeded futures and three plausible versions of the organization. Decisions are scored in dollars at the stakeholders' stated valuations; forecasts are scored on the effect of each change relative to doing nothing. Ten models made 280 attempts across 14 organizations. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, improved on doing nothing by 6.8% of the no-change cost and made 77% less forecast error than a forecaster who always predicts no effect. title: Metadata-Driven AI: An Architectural Pattern for Sustainable Data Analysis with LLMs
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) let users analyse data in natural language, either by giving the data to the model to read directly or by having the model generate code to process it. Both routes send the data, or fragments of it, to the model; both pay for inference on every run; and the code a model writes to answer a question is usually discarded once the question is answered. We present Metadata-Driven AI, an architectural pattern that keeps the data away from the model and turns each analysis into a reusable program. Only metadata (not the actual data) crosses a one-way inference boundary to the LLM. The program the LLM returns runs next to the data and is kept, so that inference is paid once per analysis rather than once per run. We describe the pattern together with a simple cost model, a measurement of how little information crosses the boundary on public datasets, and a benchmark showing that a small, locally hosted model can serve as the generator. title: FinTech and European Bank Performance: A Machine-Learning Analysis of Greenwashing and Sustainability Channels
abstract: The parallel diffusion of financial technology and the tightening of European sustainable-finance regulation have reshaped banking, yet how digitalisation affects financial performance remains unclear. Using a panel of 90 European banks over 2014–2025 (1080 bank-year observations) and a Fintech index built from annual-report text through a Dynamic Factor Model, we examine whether, and through which channels, Fintech adoption is associated with bank performance, focusing on two mechanisms usually treated as controls: greenwashing and substantive ESG practices. We combine causal mediation, a sensitivity analysis to hidden confounding, a doubly robust Double Machine Learning estimator, unconditional-quantile (RIF) regressions, Local Projections, a Causal Forest, and optimal policy learning. Four findings emerge. First, Fintech’s direct effect raises long-term soundness while depressing short-term profitability, though its total effect on profitability is insignificant. abstract: Technical white paper (v1.0, November 2026). Enterprise adoption of agentic AI is moving autonomous software from advisory roles into payments, ERP, supply chains, clinical systems and plant operations. Most agent security controls evaluate whether a single identity may perform a single action. This paper argues that the dominant failure mode of the next phase of enterprise AI is different: harmful business outcomes produced by agents that hold valid credentials and act within their permissions, either because they were manipulated or because several individually authorized agents compose into an outcome nobody approved. title: The Emergence of Agentic Finance: Reimagining Financial Intermediation
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Autonomous AI agents (software that perceives, reasons, plans, and acts toward a goal with limitedhuman intervention) are moving into the everyday plumbing of money. When consumers delegatenegotiation, allocation, or purchase execution to an agent that communicates directly with banksand payment rails, the architecture of financial intermediation is stressed at its core. This paperdefines agentic finance as the regime in which agents become the primary interface and executionlayer between consumers and providers, and asks how that regime could reconfigure the functionsintermediaries perform. Drawing on intermediation theory, I argue that agentic finance is betterunderstood as a reallocate-and-reintermediate shock than as simple disintermediation: value andcontrol migrate toward whoever owns the orchestration layer, the credential rails, and the trustinfrastructure, potentially producing new gatekeepers rather than none. abstract: Governance of agentic AI systems depends on execution evidence: an operator can judge whether an agent stayed within its authority only if its telemetry allows what it did to be reconstructed. The Governance Observability Index (GOI) proposes to measure this as a gated geometric mean of coverage, fidelity, integrity and timeliness, with an integrity gate intended to stop untrustworthy evidence being masked by completeness elsewhere. This simulation study tests one implementation of the index against criteria computed from complete ground truth, of which the estimator sees only a 40-record ledger sample. A seeded testbed simulates a scripted payments agent, a policy gateway, an authoritative ledger and an HMAC-chained telemetry stream. The estimator uses only the stream, a gateway control total and a 40-record ledger sample. Twelve fault families—four within the original specification, four outside it and four benign infrastructure perturbations—are evaluated in 2,520 single-family runs and 1,000 mixed runs. abstract: This study examines the Chinese banking sector over the period 2010–2022 and constructs a bank-level fintech index alongside a macro-level digital finance measure. Using generalised method of moments and panel threshold models, it investigates the relationship between competition, fintech, and bank stability inefficiency. The results indicate a significant non-linear effect of competition on risk, supporting the competition–stability hypothesis. Threshold analyses identify single- and double-threshold effects for capital adequacy and diversification. At the fintech level, macro-level development is associated with a significant reduction in bank risk and exhibits stronger effects than bank-level fintech. In contrast, bank-level fintech appears to mitigate risk only under specific conditions (e.g. high capitalisation or strong competition), suggesting context-dependent effects. abstract: Introduction/Main Objectives: This paper examines systemic risk interconnections within Indonesia's Non-Bank Financial Industry (NBFI), which displays intricate systemic risk interconnections that alter traditional macroprudential dynamics. As financial ecosystems digitalize, understanding cross-sectoral risk transmission beyond banking is crucial for stability. The study further aims to develop a transparent artificial intelligence framework capable of supporting timely macroprudential policy interventions and institutional decision-making. title: Verifiable Incentives: Identity-Bound Contracts and Collusion-Proof Delegation for Agent Commerce
abstract: Personal agents are entering commerce. Industry protocols now let an agent prove, cryptographically, whom it represents and what it may do, while agent wallets give it a real budget, a payment trail, and one-time merchant credentials. These are usually read as security features. We argue they are something more: the missing infrastructure for incentive contracts. When identity, authority, budget, and payment are verifiable, the principal can contract on them-and the agent's incentives change. We formalize verifiable delegation, model a three-party market of user, agent, and merchant, and derive three results: (i) verifiable identity lowers the bonus and tenure needed to sustain effort; (ii) auditable payments bound merchant collusion, with collusion becoming unprofitable as audit probability rises; and (iii) a posted honesty stake substitutes for monitoring, with the required stake decreasing in audit quality and penalty credibility. title: Target's Turnaround Is Real. Is It Agent-Ready?

abstract: This work assesses Target Corporation’s third-quarter 2026 results (reported November 18, 2026) as a test of whether a large mass-merchandise retailer is ready for agentic commerce, meaning product discovery and purchasing carried out by AI shopping agents. The analysis first separates operating performance from one-time effects. Comparable sales grew 5.6% on a 5.0% traffic gain, but about $2.14 per share of year-to-date tariff refunds account for nearly four-fifths of the raised full-year EPS outlook. On a two-year basis, store comparable sales sit less than one point above 2024. It then examines how agents see a retailer. Gains in on-shelf availability, AI-driven replenishment and price investment strengthen the attributes agents screen on first. abstract: Intelligent decision automation promises faster Saudi public and banking services, yet automating a task is not equivalent to governing a decision. This critical integrative review examines how robotic process automation, business process management and human oversight can be combined without weakening procedural fairness, operational resilience or accountability. Thirty peer reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025 are synthesised alongside the institutional context of Vision 2030, including digital government, regulated finance and electricity related service workflows. The analysis differentiates interface automation from process orchestration and consequential decision authority, and develops an original layered governance architecture with risk dependent human intervention, traceable rules and continuous process assurance. title: AI Readiness, Adoption, and Productivity: Firm-Level Evidence from Low- and Middle-Income Countries
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Can firms in developing economies translate readiness for artificial intelligence (AI) into higher productivity and greater AI adoption? This paper develops Firm-Level AI Enablement Index (FAEI), a composite measure of Power Reliability, Digital Connectivity, Human Capital, and Institutional Environment. Using World Bank Enterprise Survey data for 44,251 firms across 76 low- and middle-income economies and a 2026 follow-up covering 3,579 firms in seven economies, the analysis examines the relationship between readiness, adoption, and productivity. The findings are as follows. First, the FAEI is strongly associated with labour productivity. A 0.1 increase in FAEI is associated with 11.5 percent higher sales per worker, conditional on country, sector, and survey-year fixed effects. Second, Human Capital shows the strongest positive association among the four pillars, followed by Power Reliability and Digital Connectivity. Third, FAEI is not consistently associated with AI adoption. title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
abstract: Predictive artificial intelligence (AI) models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice, the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here, we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. title: A Three-Factor Hull-White Scenario Generator for Macro-Financial Stress Forecasting
abstract: This paper builds a scenario engine that maps a yield-curve path into a distribution of macro-financial outcomes. A three-factor Hull-White model generates arbitrage-free curves whose factors are simulated under the physical measure, with an estimated and reported market price of risk. A Minnesota-prior VARX maps the simulated curves into weekly equity returns, the federal funds rate, the Weekly Economic Index, inflation and a bank Marginal Expected Shortfall proxy, with a sign-restricted policy shock adapted to weekly data. Evaluated out of sample from 2017 to 2024, the term-structure block has the lowest forecast error in 13 of 20 maturity and horizon cells, and the density forecasts are well calibrated for the continuously moving variables. At weekly frequency the curve carries no incremental information about these variables once their own lags are controlled for, so the engine's value lies in conditioning on a specified curve path, which no benchmark can do.

abstract: When looking for a place to eat, how much do recommendations on your smartphone influence your choice? Can they help restaurants tucked away on side streets thrive in an age of algorithmic recommendations? We studied the launch of a location-based recommendation feature on South Korea’s largest search platform, tracking 16,720 restaurants over eight months. We find that visibility matters, but its benefits are uneven. Restaurants tucked away on side streets, far from subway stops, attracted the most additional attention when recommended by the algorithm. Yet this advantage did not translate into greater intentions to visit. Making a restaurant easier to discover did not necessarily overcome the inconvenience of reaching it. Digital information helped bridge this online-to-offline friction. Hard-to-reach restaurants with stronger online reputations and richer information, including customer reviews, photos, and menus, were better able to turn attention into visit intentions. title: Impact of Data Privacy Regulations on Recommender Systems Performance
abstract: Data protection regulations like GDPR and CCPA let consumers delete personal data or opt out of collection, but companies struggle to understand how these practices affect their recommendation systems. This matters because recommendations drive substantial revenue; according to industry reports, Netflix’s system saves more than $1 billion annually, and personalized suggestions generate 35% of Amazon purchases. We analyzed how different data privacy practices impact recommendation accuracy using large-scale simulations with real-world data. A critical finding: Context matters enormously. For services where user preferences are more stable (e.g., streaming platforms), opting out barely affects recommendation quality while deleting data cuts performance dramatically. However, for platforms where preferences and needs can change frequently (e.g., e-commerce), deleting old data can actually improve recommendations while opting out severely harms them. For policymakers, this means one-size-fits-all regulations may be counterproductive. A reference implementation was built and evaluated in a controlled three node Kubernetes testbed. Two workflows, healthcare eligibility determination and card payment fraud triage, were selected by purposive sampling, and ten thousand simulated requests were replayed per configuration. venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Checkout pages ask the buyer to make declarations: that they are the cardholder, that they have read the terms of sale, that a typed name is their signature. An AI agent that completes a checkout for a customer meets the same wording. This report gives three small measurements, 1,813 recorded test purchases in total, made in November 2026 in a fictional test store that logs every form it receives. (1) With eight commercial language models behind a simple text agent, the agent confirmed a bank-style step worded "By confirming, you declare that you are the cardholder" in 125 of 560 purchases. title: PRACTICAL ANALYSIS OF THE LEVEL OF ADOPTION OF OPEN BANKING AND API TECHNOLOGIES IN COMMERCIAL BANKS
venue: International journal of technology and academic research
abstract: This article presents an applied and empirical analysis of the adoption of Open Banking and Application Programming Interface (API) technologies in commercial banks. The study examines digital transformation in Uzbekistan’s banking sector, integration between banks and FinTech companies, and indicators of technological readiness using comparative analysis and a scoring-based assessment. The findings indicate that digital banks and neobanks demonstrate greater adaptability to Open API infrastructure, while monolithic IT architectures and the lack of unified national standards remain major barriers for large traditional banks. The article also presents a SWOT analysis of the Open Banking model and develops practical recommendations for introducing unified national API standards, strengthening cybersecurity, and improving consent management systems.

title: Signed but Unbound: The Authority Gap Between Agent Commerce Mandates and Crypto Wallet Signatures
abstract: When an artificial intelligence agent pays with a stablecoin, the commerce protocol can specify the merchant, order, amount, and facilitator. The token contract enforces the fields the wallet signs. We call the difference the authority gap, define nine constraint classes, and derive them for 12 authorization configurations, including Coinbase's deployed Commerce Payments Protocol. All 31,800 trials on local copies of deployed contract code match the derivation. A controlled comparison shows that committing the terms in the signed nonce binds the order. When the facilitator submits a payment to a merchant account without code, binding the facilitator requires a separate recipient contract. Of 26,653 sampled USD Coin authorizations redeemed on Base, 98.7% followed a path that any holder of the signature could redeem. We prove sufficient conditions for a recipient contract to enforce the signed mandate under a trusted signer and show which recipient a wallet displays. title: Signed, Valid, and Unauthorized: Authority Closure at the Trust Boundary Between Agent Commerce Protocols and Crypto Wallets
abstract: Agent commerce protocols let software agents pay with stablecoins. A buyer approves a payee, asset, spending cap and time window, but the wallet signs an object whose effects depend on the contracts that consume it. Matching the displayed fields or simulating one payment can miss transfers that the signed object still permits. We define authority closure as the set of transfer sequences that holding the signed object can enable. A wallet object respects the mandate when every such sequence meets the buyer's constraints. We characterize when wallet objects can satisfy this property and implement Closure, a wallet-side checker covering 13 families of signed objects. In an evaluation of 2,130 generated objects and 62,979 execution programs, 265 objects with an observed violation passed both a field-and-expiry check and an address allow-list. Under the test model, Closure rejected all 1,680 objects with an observed violation and accepted the remaining 450. In two local checkouts using the x402 reference client, approved payments settled and Closure refused requests outside the mandate before signing. The median decision time was at most 12 microseconds per family.

title: GCP: A Safety-Aware, Payment-Agnostic Commerce Protocol for Automotive and Mobility Agents
abstract: Personal agents are moving from conversation to commerce. Emerging protocols such as Poppy, UCP, and ACP define how an agent proves whom it represents, discovers merchants, fills a cart, and completes an online checkout. None of them is designed for the commerce that automotive and mobility users actually need: buying a brake pad that fits a specific VIN, booking maintenance at an authorized dealer, binding insurance, or placing a vehicle reservation under safety and consumer-protection rules. This paper proposes GCP 1.0 , an open, capability-based commerce protocol for automotive and mobility agents. GCP adds four things that general commerce protocols lack: (i) vehicle context and safety gates as first-class protocol objects; (ii) a delegation and authorization ladder that lets a human grant bounded purchase authority and revoke it at any time; (iii) a payment-agnostic intent layer that abstracts card, wallet, Alipay, WeChat Pay, OEM finance, and agent-native payment tokens; and (iv) a typed exception and recovery model for the failure modes of real commerce. title: Recognised ROI: A Routing Identity and Recognition Rule for Measuring the Return on AI Efficiency Gains
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Organisations commonly report the return on artificial intelligence by multiplying the hours a tool saves by a fully loaded labour rate. Field experiments support the first half of that calculation: generative AI releases measurable capacity on many tasks. The best available administrative evidence does not support the second half. In linked Danish records, earnings, recorded hours, employment and wage bills have so far moved little, and the chief financial officer of a major bank has said that the benefits are not observable in its quarterly earnings. This paper argues that the gap is not only a measurement lag to be waited out. It is also the predictable result of pricing a reduction in resource usage as though it were a reduction in resource spending, an error that management accounting resolved more than three decades ago. The paper proposes the Recognised ROI model. abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved widespread adoption across the financial sector, pure neural architectures still suffer from inherent stochasticity, creating severe bottlenecks in mission-critical, zero-tolerance operations such as corporate syndicated lending, cross-asset portfolio stress testing, and regulatory compliance. Currently, financial institutions rely heavily on costly frontier generalist LLMs, which are plagued by numerical hallucinations, black-box opacity, lack of auditability, and cloud data-leakage risks. Furthermore, because these models rely on surface-level statistical correlations, they are highly susceptible to spurious correlations and confounding biases. title: The Economics of Instant Payments: A Structured, Evidence-Graded Review of Financial Inclusion, Welfare, and Macro-Financial Effects across Global Fast-Payment Systems
abstract: Purpose: This article examines the economic consequences of instant payment systems (financial inclusion, welfare, growth and macro-financial stability) and seeks to separate the well-established effects from the projections and correlations that form the basis of much of the practitioner discussion. Methodology: This is a structured narrative review. The evidence is synthesized under an explicit four-tier scheme that gives primacy to peer-reviewed causal studies and central bank research over industry reports, separates out the observed from the forecasted, and places causal identification at the heart of the analysis. The review draws on 22 sources published between 2014 and 2026. The four systems under review are Brazil's Pix, India's UPI, the US FedNow and RTP and the EU's SEPA Instant. These are compared on design features. Findings: The best-evidenced finding is microeconomic: mobile-money access is estimated to have lifted around 2% of Kenyan households out of poverty and there are quasi-experimental findings on the impact of adoption in Mexico and India. The aggregate GDP and consumer savings data are all based on industry estimates and should be treated as indicative only.

abstract: This study investigates whether and how digital transformation affects the credit risk of commercial banks in Yemen, where protracted conflict, institutional fragmentation, and severe data constraints complicate the operation and evaluation of the banking system. Using a balanced branch-level panel of 42 branches from two representative Banks over 2013–2024, we construct a composite digital transformation index (DDT) covering digital management, digital business, and digital strategy, and measure credit risk primarily by the Z-score, with the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio as a robustness proxy. The Z-score is constructed in its conventional form, in which higher values denote a greater distance from insolvency and therefore lower credit risk; all regressions were re-estimated with the corrected measure and every reported sign has been reassessed accordingly. Fixed-effects regressions show that digital transformation significantly reduces credit risk, while model fit improves (R² from 0.209 to 0.303). title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
abstract: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

title: Separating AI from Capital: Identifying the Productivity Contribution of Artificial Intelligence across Countries and Sectors
abstract: Does enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) raise total factor productivity (TFP), or does measured output growth mainly reflect capital deepening and labour growth? We separate these channels in two stages. title: Reviewed Before It Runs: Automated Review of an Architect's Authority
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AI agents are granted authority in two layers: a boundary written in advance for a whole deployment, and a decision on each action as it arrives, made by a person or, increasingly, by a classifier model. Neither states what one task needs before it runs. We study an alternative, in which each task’s authority is written down before anything runs and reviewed there. title: The Three Laws of Payment Physics: Speed-Finality Separation, Friction Relocation, and Multilateral Liquidity-Saving Netting Across Global Retail and Wholesale Rails
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Modern electronic checkouts complete contactless card authorizations and mobile QR scans in 150 to 400 milliseconds, sustaining the widespread illusion that sovereign purchasing power moves at fiber-optic speed. In reality, global financial plumbing separates fast cryptographic messaging from irrevocable balance-sheet extinction across commercial and central bank ledgers. Bridging monetary economics with protocol-level distributed systems engineering, this 8-page open-access working paper (Digbijoy Labs Working Paper WP-2026-03) formalizes The Three Laws of Payment Physics: Law I — The Speed–Finality Divide: Authorization messages record conditional intent at fiber-optic speed, whereas interbank debt extinguishes only when central-bank reserves (Tier 0 M0) or statutory settlement assets mutate across nested double-entry ledgers. venue: International Journal of Economics Management and Accounting (IJEMA)
abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots in e-commerce has restructured customer service delivery. However, online shoppers frequently experience pre-purchase decision hesitation due to transaction uncertainties. Grounded in Uncertainty Reduction Theory and Social Response Theory, this study investigates how Conversational AI Responsiveness and Perceived Anthropomorphism mitigate Customer Decision Hesitation through the mediating role of Brand Trust. Data were collected via an online survey from 195 e-commerce consumers in Indonesia who interacted with AI chatbots during their shopping journeys. The empirical framework was evaluated using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. abstract: On 16 November 2026, an attacker who had gained access to the Optimizely experimentation platform wrote malicious JavaScript into the projects of 178 organisations, and most of their websites served it to visitors for about 16 hours. The payload loaded a second-stage script from an attacker host, carried an obfuscated inline copy that executes through eval when that host is blocked, skimmed payment card data, swapped cryptocurrency addresses, and sent stolen data to the attacker host, card data through navigator.sendBeacon. title: Separating Automation Gains from Agent Contributions in AI-Assisted Model Validation
abstract: LLM agents are being proposed for bank model validation, yet evaluations that compare agent-assisted work with manual practice credit the agent with gains that come from digitized evidence and deterministic tests. We propose a staged architecture in which an LLM-free controlled workflow (P1) is both the fallback and the control arm for individually authorized agent tasks (P2), and an attribution protocol that credits an agent only for faults P1 does not already report. title: JevRisk: Zero-Shot Financial Risk Assessment with a Language Decision Model
abstract: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. Second, the language decision model (e.g., \jev{}) reads these indicators together with the customer's profile and activity, judges the case in context with broad world knowledge, and returns the score of high risk. title: Know Your Context Bank: Repairing Inconsistency and Measuring Generalization in Context-Aware Text-to-SQL
abstract: Text-to-SQL systems increasingly rely on context banks: curated collections of example queries, metric definitions, and domain knowledge that tell a model how an organization writes its queries. In the enterprise, a bank grows over years as many analysts add entries, checked one at a time for correctness (does the SQL answer its own question?) and rarely for consistency with one another. Yet correctness is often loosely defined: a question seldom fixes how an entity is counted or which table defines it, so two entries can each pass review yet resolve the same decision in opposite ways. We call this condition context bank rot. A second question follows: does a system that uses a bank generalize from it, or only reproduce it? Existing benchmarks cannot tell, as they do not control how far a test question sits from the context. title: Competition in capital markets and its contribution to growth and innovation
venue: OECD competition law and policy working papers.
abstract: Financing conditions influence whether innovative firms can enter, expand and constrain established suppliers. Competition in capital markets can therefore affect innovation and productivity across the economy, as well as conditions in financial markets. This paper examines competition in equity investment in unlisted innovative firms, focussing on independent venture capital, corporate venture capital, private equity and equity crowdfunding. Bank finance, public equity markets, market infrastructure and intermediary services are covered where they offer workable alternatives or affect private financing or exit options. The paper assesses whether firms have credible alternatives that constrain capital providers on financial, governance and strategic terms, and how choice changes over the financing lifecycle. It distinguishes financing constraints arising from the risks of innovation from restrictions on competition among providers and intermediaries. title: Held-to-Maturity Accounting: Hidden Losses and Systemic Fragility
abstract: This paper studies how accounting-induced opacity affects systemic risk in the banking system. Motivated by the buildup of unrealized losses during recent monetary tightening episodes, we develop a model in which banks hold correlated interest rate sensitive assets and are connected through an endogenous interbank network. We show that Held-To-Maturity (HTM) accounting amplifies systemic risk by delaying loss recognition, allowing losses to accumulate and become synchronized across institutions. When losses are realized under liquidity stress, the interaction of correlated exposures and network linkages generates nonlinear increases in defaults. These findings suggest that accounting regimes are not neutral from a financial stability perspective, as they influence both the buildup and propagation of systemic risk, particularly in environments with common asset exposures and strong interconnectedness.

title: Reward Integrity in Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for LLM Guardrail Red-Teaming
abstract: We study reward fidelity in an adversarial reinforcement-learning loop for red-teaming financial-services language-model guardrails. Apparent wins can arise when an attack omits prescribed personally identifiable information (PII), or when a reward judge credits a response that did not break the targeted policy. On attacker-generated and public benchmark examples, TypeSafe Jev checks whether the prescribed PII is present. For outcome scoring, we compare the decision models TypeSafe Jev, Laya (pretrained and post-trained), and pretrained CLM-8B with logged Opus 4.8 judgements from a replay corpus. Post-training markedly improves Laya's agreement with the judge. A separate author-reviewed off-target set establishes that Opus can award false wins. The findings motivate specialised decision-model judges for checking prescribed PII in attack inputs and scoring target responses against the intended policy.

abstract: An agent built on a large language model (LLM) can write a wrong value into a database while every signal reports success: the value has a valid format, the database accepts it, the write returns success, and the agent's explanation raises no flag. This paper measures how often this happens when the value is a computed financial amount. The reference is computed by deterministic code from Central Bank of Brazil series, and each value is read back from four database engines. title: Willingness to Use and Actual Use of e-CNY: Mediation Mechanisms Within a Mature Payment Ecosystem
abstract: The e-CNY pilot programs have expanded steadily in recent years, reflecting China’s continued efforts to promote its central bank digital currency (CBDC). However, actual use of the e-CNY remains low in China’s mature payment ecosystem. This study examines the antecedents of willingness to use and actual use of the e-CNY and their mediation pathways by extending the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) with trust, perceived risk, and innovation resistance. Data were collected from 509 respondents and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and explainable machine learning. PLS-SEM was employed to examine the effects of the antecedents on willingness to use and actual use and to identify their mediation types. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was used to assess their relative predictive importance. title: Agentic AI Risk Management: Governance Protocols for Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems in Financial Services
abstract: The financial services sector is undergoing a fundamental transformation as institutions transition from reactive, prompt-based AI systems toward autonomous, goal-directed agentic architectures. Unlike prior AI deployments requiring structured inputs and continuous human oversight, agentic systems plan, reason, and execute complex multi-step workflows with minimal intervention. By 2026, adoption of agentic AI in financial operations is projected to exceed 600% growth, with global market spend approaching $50 billion and potential productivity gains of $3 trillion. This rapid deployment introduces a new class of systemic risks—including cascading failures, algorithmic collusion, adversarial prompt injection, and goal inversion—that existing governance frameworks are ill-equipped to address. This paper proposes the Agentic Trust Framework (ATF), a comprehensive governance architecture for monitoring, containing, and auditing autonomous agent workflows in financial institutions. title: GuardRail: Runtime Action Authorization and Behavioral Safety for Agentic AI Systems
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: LLM agents no longer only produce text: they call APIs, query databases, send messages, and initiate payments. The safety mechanisms deployed around them, however, still operate mainly on text. They screen the prompt going in and the response coming out, while the agent's plan, the ordered sequence of tool calls it is about to execute, runs unchecked. That gap is exploitable: instructions planted in a web page, email, or tool result can steer the plan toward actions the user never intended, and an agent can alter an action after it has been approved. title: Impact of Open Finance Data Sharing on Credit Access for Unbanked and Underbanked Populations: A Systematic Review
abstract: In addition to being a great means of increasing financial literacy, open finance data sharing has proven itself to be a crucial instrument for enhancing financial inclusion through providing greater access to formal loans. This paper represents a systematic literature review based on a comprehensive analysis of 80 empirical articles written between 2009 and 2026 in different countries across five continents and related to the effects of open finance on the formal credit market. The analysis shows that open finance always positively impacts the probability of receiving loans but does not affect the extent of such an impact. If a country has developed credit bureau infrastructure, the probability of receiving formal loans increases by 3–9%, while in countries where people do not have any formal credit history, the probabilities usually go up by 15–30 percentage points or even higher. abstract: This study examines the impact of Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) adoption on cross-border payment efficiency in Nigeria using a Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) framework. The eNaira, launched by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) in October 2021, represents Africa's first retail CBDC. Using quarterly data from 2010:Q1 to 2024:Q4, we estimate a medium-scale DSGE model incorporating financial frictions, cross-border payment costs, and CBDC adoption dynamics. The Bayesian estimation results indicate that CBDC adoption shocks significantly improve cross-border payment efficiency, reduce exchange rate volatility, and enhance remittance inflows. title: Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI): Emerging Challenges and Issues in International Financial Law
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Digital public infrastructure is slowly becoming the base for many financial services. It includes systems such as digital identity, instant payments, and sharing of financial data with consent. These systems help people receive government benefits, make payments, and open bank accounts more easily. But they also bring legal problems, especially when personal data, private companies, and cross-border transactions are involved. This paper looks at the legal issues connected with digital public infrastructure in international financial law. At present, there is no one international law that covers DPI completely. Payments, data protection, cybersecurity, and digital identity are handled under different laws in different countries. Because of this, companies and users face confusion when a DPI-based service works across borders. The paper studies India, the European Union, and Brazil. These three examples show that countries are building DPI in different ways, but the law has not developed at the same speed. title: Artificial Intelligence and Credit Scoring: Opportunities, Ethical Challenges, and Regulatory Implications
abstract: The aim of this study is to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is changing credit scoring and to assess the opportunities, ethical concerns, and regulatory challenges associated with its use. It traces the shift from traditional statistical models to AI-based approaches, reviews machine learning, neural networks, and deep learning techniques, and compares their main characteristics with conventional scoring methods. It also considers the safeguards needed for responsible adoption. The study draws on a narrative review of academic literature and regulatory documents, including the European Union’s Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI and the AI Act, alongside a qualitative comparison of credit scoring approaches. The findings suggest that AI can help lenders capture nonlinear relationships, use alternative data, assess applications more quickly, and reach borrowers with limited credit histories. These benefits, however, depend on the quality of the data and how models are validated and used. title: An Explainable Artificial Intelligence Framework for Customer Churn Management and Retention Decision Support in Service Operations
abstract: Customer churn prediction is a critical task for service-oriented firms because customer loss directly affects revenue stability, customer lifetime value, and long-term profitability. Although machine learning models can identify customers who are likely to churn, many existing approaches emphasize predictive accuracy without sufficiently explaining churn drivers or translating predictions into actionable retention strategies. To address this limitation, this study proposes an explainable AI-driven multi-dataset churn management framework that integrates machine learning prediction, SHAP-based explainability, probability-based risk segmentation, and counterfactual retention strategy simulation. The framework is evaluated using three publicly available customer churn datasets from telecommunications and banking contexts: IBM Telco, Orange Telecom, and Banking Churn. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost are trained and compared using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and AUC-PR. The results show that model performance varies across datasets, with XGBoost achieving strong performance on Orange Telecom and Random Forest performing competitively on Banking Churn

title: Delegated Loyalty: Fiduciary Duties and Commercial Conflicts in Personal AI Agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Delegation transfers a decision without transferring loyalty. Commercial AI providers now market personal agents that search, compare, negotiate, and buy on a user's behalf. The same providers collect merchant fees on completed purchases, sell conversation-matched advertising, and run retail stores whose goods the agent can recommend. In the early 1980s, airline reservation systems presented the same conflict, ranking the owning carrier's flights first. Federal regulators answered with rules against display bias. Common-law agency forbids undisclosed third-party benefits and adverse-party dealing, yet treats software as a tool incapable of owing duties. Any duty attaches to the provider. Seven duties follow from agency doctrine and from broker, search, and online marketplace rules. Those duties require loyalty to declared interests, conflict disclosure, a bar on undisclosed commissions, transparent ranking separated from advertising, audit trails, and portability. Without these duties, a commercial personal agent operates as the provider's representative inside the user's decisions. Keywords: Personal AI Agents, Agentic Commerce, Fiduciary Duty, Duty of Loyalty, Conflict-of-Interes

title: Measuring Brand Visibility in Agentic Commerce Through Citation Share, Basket Capture, and Paid-Presence Transfer in Consumer Packaged Goods
venue: Journal of Marketing & Supply Chain Management
abstract: Generative assistants and shopping agents increasingly choose which consumer packaged goods (CPG) brands shoppers see, yet no published study has measured brand visibility in these habitual, repeat-purchase categories. This paper introduces a reproducible measurement framework built on five constructs: Citation Share (with a rank-weighted variant), the probability that a brand is named for a brand-free query; Basket Capture Rate, the share of agent-assembled basket items won by one manufacturer; Portfolio Halo, the gain in a manufacturer’s chance of winning a basket slot after winning the previous one; Source Provenance Ratio, the mix of cited domain classes; and the Paid-Presence Index, a count of visible sponsored placements that does not measure advertising spend. All data are simulated. title: The Agent's Receipt: What an Audit Trail Must Contain When No Human Watched
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: When an AI agent buys something on a customer's behalf, no human watches the purchase. The customer does not see the options, does not hear the reasoning, and cannot describe what happened if the purchase goes wrong. The dispute process, built for human buyers, has no witness to call. This paper proposes the minimum audit trail an agent purchase must leave behind: five records that together let a person who was not present reconstruct what happened and decide who bears the cost. The five records are the mandate record, which captures the customer's instruction as the agent understood it; the reasoning record, which captures what the agent considered and why it chose; the authorization record, which captures the scoped permission for this one purchase; the transaction record, which captures what was actually bought, from whom, and at what price; and the outcome record, which captures what happened after, including objections, corrections, and refunds. title: PRACTICAL ANALYSIS OF BANK CUSTOMER BEHAVIOR AND SERVICE DELIVERY CHANNELS IN THE OPEN BANKING ENVIRONMENT
venue: International journal of technology and academic research
abstract: This article presents an applied and empirical analysis of changes in the behavior of commercial bank customers and in service delivery channels as the Open Banking ecosystem takes shape. The study assesses the shift from traditional bank channels to FinTech and open API platforms, customer preferences, and service efficiency indicators (transaction share, customer reach growth, operating cost, and customer satisfaction index) for 2024–2026. The findings show that the share of transactions made through Open API channels has reached 52%, and that serving customers through traditional branches costs more than 30 times as much as through open digital channels. The article identifies the main barriers (cybersecurity and trust, the digital literacy gap, and fragmented user experience) and develops strategic recommendations for banks: developing a hybrid omnichannel model, increasing the transparency of consent management, and personalized API monetization.

title: Machine Learning-Based Customer Segmentation and Tailored Financial Advice in the Banking Sector
abstract: Customer segmentation in banking involves grouping customers into distinct segments who exhibit similar behaviors, such as transaction frequency, spending patterns, and savings habits. This enables banks to target their offerings more effectively. This study applied an unsupervised machine learning approach using the K-means clustering algorithm to segment customers. The analysis was based on secondary data comprising 100,000 customers. The silhouette score peaked at k = 3 with a score of 0.3232, but based on the Elbow method and aiming for a potentially more granular segmentation, k = 5 was chosen. The identified customer segments were: established female savers; recently active engagers (mostly male); low-balance, less-active males; core male customers; and a high-value, high-activity segment. To further refine the segmentation, RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) analysis was implemented to reveal customer behaviors within each cluster, resulting in more precise customer profiling. This dual-layer approach enables banks to develop personalized marketing strategies and improve customer relationship management.

title: Privacy-Preserving AI in Finance: Federated Learning, Secure Computation, and GDPR Compliance for Fraud Detection and Credit Scoring
abstract: Financial institutions need large datasets to build AI systems, yet they must protect sensitive customer information under regimes such as the GDPR. This review examines how federated learning, secure multi-party computation, homomorphic encryption, and differential privacy support privacy-preserving AI in financial services. It covers the principles of data sovereignty, federated architectures for enterprise systems, and applications in cross-institutional collaboration, fraud detection, credit scoring, and personalized banking. It also discusses regulatory compliance, auditability, adversarial robustness, and cyber resilience. The literature indicates that these techniques help institutions meet data minimization requirements, reduce legal risk, and collaborate across borders. Trade-offs remain in computational overhead, latency, non-IID data, and model bias. Future work should focus on standardized protocols, hybrid privacy models, and auditing frameworks.

title: Learning from a Biased Sample
abstract: The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. title: Deep Tangency Portfolio
abstract: We develop a deep learning framework to directly estimate tangency portfolio weights by augmenting benchmark factors with a long-short deep factor derived from high-dimensional characteristics. Guided by a Sharpe ratio maximization objective, the deep factor plays two key roles: (i) providing a natural hedge against benchmark risks and (ii) capturing multimarket signals to enhance the performance of the benchmark. In an empirical application to U.S. corporate bonds using 132 firm-level bond, equity, and option characteristics, the deep factor achieves an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio exceeding one, and the deep tangency portfolio benchmarked against the market factor yields a Sharpe ratio over two, outperforming portfolios spanned by common observable or latent factors. These results demonstrate that bond risk signals are fundamentally dense, requiring the nonlinear integration of multimarket information to span the efficient frontier. title: Can Open LLMs Clear Sanctions-Screening Alerts? A Pre-registered Test on Public Sanctions Lists with Turkish Name Variants
abstract: Sanctions screening raises name-based alerts that are mostly false positives, and level-1 analysts clear them by checking the customer's date of birth and name against a written policy. We test whether open-weight language models that a bank can run on its own premises can perform this level-1 disposition. From the UK and EU sanctions lists (7,103 natural persons) we built 12,200 synthetic customers: listed persons under six name conditions, including Turkish spellings of Arabic-origin names and Turkish romanisations of Cyrillic names, and two date-of-birth conditions, plus namesakes, near-name customers and a general population. A deterministic fuzzy and embedding screen raised 7,383 alerts, which three open models served on domestic infrastructure and three rule baselines dispositioned under the same policy. Independent Execution Authorization for AI Agents: Separating the authority to permit an action from the system that proposes it
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AI agents are moving from answering questions to taking actions: they make payments, change records, grant access and commit organizations to third parties. Holding a credential is not the same as being authorized to take a specific action at a specific moment. This position paper defines independent execution authorization: the decision, made immediately before an AI agent's action takes effect, on whether that specific action is permitted to execute, made outside the trust domain of the system taking the action. It grounds the idea in established security principles (separation of privilege, complete mediation, fail-safe defaults), sets out six requirements (independence, action specificity, fail-closed, no route around it, verifiable evidence, every applicable authority), distinguishes it from identity and access management, policy-based authorization, platform gateways, guardrails, agent security and observability, and states its limits. The system taking the action cannot be the system authorizing the action, and if the check cannot run, the action does not. title: Now You See Me Now You Don't: A Framework To Detect and Reduce Proxy Capacity
abstract: In regulated domains such as lending, the two most salient fairness concepts are disparate impact and disparate treatment: disparate impact is generally defined by differential rates of adverse outcomes between demographic groups, while disparate treatment is generally defined by the use of demographic information or proxies to issue decisions. There already exist established methods to quantitatively detect and mitigate disparate impact; however, there has been less research on doing the same for disparate treatment. From a practitioner's perspective, the manner in which a conditional independence test is formulated and operationalized to identify proxies is nuanced and underexplored. As Machine Learning (ML) systems increase in scope and application in regulated domains, practitioners need a defensible framework to identify proxies at scale. title: Technology–augmented credit creation in supply chain finance: dynamic synergy of AI, blockchain, and data assetization
abstract: The coupling of blockchain, artificial intelligence (AI), and data assetization (DA) offers a transformative pathway for supply chain finance (SCF) to alleviate financing constraints of small and medium–sized enterprises (SMEs). This study develops a tripartite evolutionary game model integrating blockchain–based certification, AI valuation correction, and dynamic incentive–penalty mechanisms for DA–backed SCF financing. title: Project financing in vanishing forests: Do investors care about nature protection?
abstract: Biodiversity risks are increasingly recognized by financial market participants, yet their measurement at the corporate-entity level obscures the locations and assets through which they arise. Project finance links identifiable physical assets to dedicated financing contracts, allowing us to examine this transmission more directly. By linking 9,037 project-loan pairs in 115 countries, we relate bank loan spreads to projects' proximity to protected areas, surrounding forest loss and lenders' nature policies. We find that lenders price proximity to protected areas only when they also have explicit nature risk policies and particularly within 1.5 km buffers from the project location. title: Fintech Expansion
abstract: I study credit market outcomes with different competing lending technologies: a fintech lender that learns from data and can seize on-platform sales, and a banking sector that relies on physical collateral. Despite flexible information acquisition technology, endogenous fintech learning is surprisingly coarse, with a single threshold that screens out low-quality borrowers. As fintech lending technology improves, better enforcement harms, while better information technology benefits traditional banking sector profits. Big data technology enables the fintech to leverage data from its early-stage operations in unbanked markets to develop predictive models that support expansion into wealthier markets. title: Understanding the Prompting Effects of Chain-of-Thought on Human Collaboration with Generative AI
abstract: It is well established that Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves model performance in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). Far less understood is whether presenting CoT reasoning in AI-enabled interfaces enhances users’ perceived trust in GenAI’s competence in performing tasks. Drawing on the Heuristic-Systematic Model, we develop a theoretical framework in which CoT presence and quality trigger either heuristic perceptions of transparency or systematic perceptions of diagnosticity and germane cognitive load, with distinct mechanisms across task-difficulty conditions. Across a series of online experiments, we identify two key findings. First, high-quality CoT consistently enhances perceived trust in GenAI’s ability to generate correct outputs, regardless of task difficulty. title: Screening, Investment Incentives, and the Welfare Trade-Offs of Privacy
abstract: This paper studies how information disclosure affects investment incentives and contracting efficiency. We analyze a class of principal-agent models in which information helps the principal screen the agent but also facilitates surplus appropriation, thereby weakening the agent’s incentive to invest before contracting. Efficient privacy regimes balance these two forces. Along the frontier of efficient information policies, more privacy is associated with stronger investment incentives and higher agent payoff. We characterize conditions under which full privacy, full disclosure, or intermediate privacy is efficient. The results provide guidance for intellectual property and innovation policy by identifying when additional privacy fosters or hinders economic efficiency and innovation. title: Impact of Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and Digital Payments on India's Economic Growth: Macroeconomic Channels, Financial Inclusion, and Structural Formalization
abstract: The rapid proliferation of digital payment architectures, anchored by the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), has triggered a structural paradigm shift in the Indian economy. abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and startup valuation in fintech and financial services firms using a sample of 287 companies with 897 funding rounds from January 2020 to June 2026. title: Self-Service Failure Recovery and Autonomous Operational Remediation in Multi-Tenant Financial Systems: A Conceptual Framework
venue: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF PURE SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
abstract: Multi-tenant financial platforms, including core banking as a service, payment processors, embedded finance providers and wealth management back offices, concentrate the operations of many regulated institutions onto shared infrastructure. When such platforms fail, the cost is measured not only in downtime but in misposted balances, duplicated payments, breached settlement windows and regulatory exposure for every tenant at once. Two operational paradigms have matured in parallel to address this: autonomous remediation, in which the platform detects and corrects faults without human intervention, and self-service recovery, in which tenants are given the tools to diagnose and resolve incidents affecting their own scope. Yet the literature treats these largely in isolation, and neither is well theorised for environments where financial integrity, tenant isolation and supervisory accountability are binding constraints. title: AgentBank: Banking on Blockchain Agentic Payments
abstract: AI agents increasingly pay for data and computation through protocols such as x402 and AP2, but individually funded wallets idle and require asset transfers for every payment. We present AgentBank, a smart-contract banking layer that lets agents spend bank liabilities under owner-issued mandates and on-chain spending limits. Internal payments update account balances without transferring assets, while pooled backing funds are allocated between reserves and yield-bearing strategies. We bound losses from compromised agent keys and analyze how correlated demand affects reserve requirements. Experiments show that AgentBank reduces idle liquidity by 52-77% relative to per-agent wallets and lowers gas costs for batched internal payments. Using historical DeFi liquidity data, we evaluate how reserve policies balance treasury returns against payment availability during market stress. We further examine the risks of automated bank runs and evaluate mechanisms to mitigate them.
